hook-0-1mbojfw.text: Everything in the universe is flying apart.

hook-1-1uh13cw.text: And here's the weird part: it's speeding up.

hook-2-mwvxrr.text: Physicists call whatever is doing this dark energy.

hook-3-1elc419.text: It's about seventy percent of everything… and nobody knows what it is.

hook-5-1ushcjw.text: What if nothing is pushing the universe apart?

problem-0-yzq4fg.text: In 1998, two teams measured distant exploding stars: type one A supernovae.

problem-1-17awbtv.text: They were too dim. Farther away than a slowing-down universe allows.

problem-2-16l73v.text: The fix: a cosmological constant, Lambda. Energy built into empty space itself.

problem-3-294bvx.text: It works beautifully. But it comes with two embarrassing problems.

problem-4-1fjx1hl.text: One: quantum physics predicts a vacuum energy about ten to the one hundred and twenty times too big.

problem-5-q03616.text: Two: why is dark energy roughly equal to matter right now, of all the moments we could be living in?

problem-6-yvdjdx.text: Fitting the data is not the same as explaining it.

beyond-1-1lwgnw2.text: Everything we can ever see is a sphere about 14 giga-parsecs in radius. Roughly 46 billion light-years.

beyond-2-y2y4k3.text: Standard cosmology assumes it looks the same out there as in here. Forever.

beyond-4-1q7v3n8.text: Picture giant dark masses far beyond our horizon, each hundreds to thousands of times heavier than our entire observable universe.

beyond-5-pb6234.text: Call them H. M. E. A. s: hyper-massive external attractors.

beyond-6-4xo81y.text: Not a neat grid: a lumpy, settled swarm, like galaxies in a relaxed cluster. Only absurdly bigger.

beyond-7-1irtfh2.text: And our universe sits in one of the gaps.

tides-0-53w15h.text: Quick gravity fact: a perfectly smooth shell of mass around you pulls on you… not at all.

tides-1-9x6hxo.text: Every direction cancels. That's Newton's shell theorem.

tides-3-1pkx7vn.text: The side of our bubble closer to a node gets pulled harder than the middle, and the middle harder than the far side.

tides-4-11eolkj.text: So the bubble gets stretched. That's a tide, the same thing the Moon does to our oceans.

tides-5-19h9gx9.text: Do the math, and the tidal pull grows in proportion to distance: two G M R over S cubed.

tides-6-8r6e8f.text: And dark energy's push? Also proportional to distance.

tides-7-95kt69.text: Same shape. To gravity, a pull from outside can look exactly like a push from inside.

numbers-0-1dee8f7.text: How heavy, and how far? Plug in the numbers.

numbers-1-1vnd6dd.text: Nodes about five hundred times our observable universe's mass…

numbers-2-7tqxzg.text: …spaced about 39 giga-parsecs apart, would do the job.

numbers-3-fz2nhx.text: No exotic vacuum energy. Just ordinary gravity, from very big things, very far away.

whatif-center-0-dccbl6.text: What if we sat exactly in the middle, with nodes evenly all around us?

whatif-center-1-19u44ea.text: Then every pull cancels. No acceleration at all.

whatif-center-2-1kfnlqn.text: And a subtle twist: in empty space, tides can’t simply inflate a volume.

whatif-center-3-816x83.text: They stretch one way and squeeze the others. Pure shear.

whatif-center-4-1k13lvc.text: The overall speed-up comes from the bubble creeping closer to the nodes, where the pull grows faster and faster.

whatif-center-5-1678qaf.text: And that leftover stretch? It’s a fingerprint. Hold that thought.

progenitor-0-r0shgp.text: But wait. Why would we be anywhere near the middle of a gap?

progenitor-1-1hz5slo.text: Here's the boldest what-if: what if the Big Bang was one of these nodes?

progenitor-2-1sk3uip.text: A node, sitting at its balance point among its neighbours…

progenitor-4-8k1q8v.text: It blows apart, and the matter expands evenly into the surrounding gap.

progenitor-5-10rmmeh.text: That explains why we start near the middle, and why the expansion looks the same in every direction.

progenitor-6-1n253q0.text: This is the Progenitor Hypothesis. And it's one mass playing two roles:

progenitor-7-57kf5x.text: before the bang, a member of the swarm. After it, everything that came out.

progenitor-8-8kg9mk.text: The most natural guess: our progenitor was just a typical node. Nothing special.

simulation-0-ivqjnc.text: Nice story. Does it actually work? Time to simulate.

simulation-1-wuq6kl.text: Thousands of particles in a cloud, and nothing but plain Newtonian gravity.

simulation-2-umory3.text: Self-gravity slows the cloud down. The distant nodes pull it apart.

simulation-3-1ps8xar.text: We start 2.9 billion years after the Big Bang, and run to today: 13.8 billion years.

simulation-4-iglhuw.text: First, a sanity check: set the node mass to zero.

simulation-5-1ojttnd.text: The simulation hands back the textbook universe with no dark energy. Exactly.

simulation-6-fm6hfu.text: Good. Now turn the nodes on.

simulation-7-173p1gd.text: The cloud grows by just the right amount. Like a universe with dark energy, but without any.

data-0-b7rc5g.text: Now the moment of truth: real data.

data-1-ntd9b0.text: Over fifteen hundred type one A supernovae from the Pantheon plus catalogue.

data-2-66xkca.text: We turn the simulated expansion into a distance-versus-redshift curve. No shortcuts.

data-3-6b6zan.text: Zoom in on the differences. A universe without dark energy misses. Badly.

data-4-12oxrgt.text: Standard Lambda C D M nails it.

data-7-lw2wnt.text: Fit score, lower is better: no dark energy, zero point eight four three. Lambda C D M, zero point four three six. Node model, zero point four four zero.

data-8-1yye1h6.text: To be clear: it matches Lambda C D M. It doesn’t beat it. And the match holds from ten thousand to a hundred thousand particles.

whatif-observer-0-1ruqtam.text: What if we're not at the centre of the cloud? We almost certainly aren't.

whatif-observer-1-rk9il8.text: So every particle gets a turn being us. Does any vantage point see our universe?

whatif-observer-2-rj7kc9.text: Plenty do. And not just in one lucky setup: many different configurations get there.

whatif-close-0-16juz35.text: What if the nodes are too close? Two things can go wrong.

whatif-close-1-zj60uk.text: The pull wins outright: a runaway that rips the cloud apart way too fast.

whatif-close-2-1ltcjmv.text: Or something sneakier: the core of the cloud collapses into a dense knot.

whatif-close-3-hamter.text: On the left, a run with a great supernova fit… and a collapsing core. On the right, a healthy one.

whatif-close-4-1hd3mkb.text: So a good fit is not enough. A universe-like run must pass a checklist:

whatif-close-5-18qkxlp.text: fit the supernovae, grow by the right amount, keep its core from collapsing, and keep every node outside our horizon.

whatif-close-6-nlwoud.text: Picking by fit alone would have chosen the collapsing universes. The checklist catches them.

whatif-close-7-1gmc41y.text: With it: 68 out of 72 configurations are universe-like.

whatif-mass-0-1kax4ys.text: What if the progenitor was tiny? Or enormous?

whatif-mass-1-14v09vb.text: We tried more than three orders of magnitude: from one observable universe, up to three thousand.

whatif-mass-2-ueos8x.text: The fit barely cares. The structure does.

whatif-mass-3-1n5jo5b.text: And the most robust choice is the typical node: exactly what the hypothesis preferred, before we ran anything.

catch-0-68878z.text: Now the catch. Because there is one.

catch-1-10t4wid.text: Heavy nodes far away, or lighter nodes closer in: the supernovae can’t tell them apart.

catch-2-1xc03rd.text: The average expansion only measures mass over spacing cubed.

catch-3-13hchtn.text: So the Hubble diagram alone will never prove this model. We need a different test.

predictions-0-14r3vqf.text: Remember the stretch fingerprint? That’s the test.

predictions-1-k0tmdp.text: Prediction one: a Hubble dipole. One half of the sky should expand a little faster than the other.

predictions-2-1vi8bi9.text: Which might feed the Hubble tension: 67 versus 73, depending on how you measure.

predictions-3-1uy5uwn.text: Prediction two: the Axis of Evil. The biggest patterns in the cosmic microwave background line up along a strange axis.

predictions-4-1v6wca4.text: Lopsided neighbours could imprint exactly that kind of alignment.

predictions-5-vx69br.text: Prediction three: dark flow. Galaxies drifting in bulk, pulled by something outside the survey.

predictions-6-1y9894a.text: Prediction four: as we near the nodes, the acceleration grows. Phantom dark energy: w below minus one.

predictions-7-bv2xu.text: And the kicker: they should all point the same way. Toward our nearest, heaviest neighbours.

whatif-invisible-0-1sv63tq.text: If these things are so huge, why can’t we see them?

whatif-invisible-1-jxqmdt.text: They're beyond our horizon, for a start. But they'd also be ancient black holes that ate everything nearby long ago.

whatif-invisible-2-1ucrz1g.text: No food, no glowing disk. Their Hawking temperature: about ten to the minus thirty-three kelvin.

whatif-invisible-3-1jfg6mg.text: Dark giants. Seen only by their pull.

whatif-cycle-0-wasfya.text: One last, wild what-if. Pure speculation: no simulation behind this one.

whatif-cycle-1-1fkwxzb.text: A node bangs. Its matter fills the gap.

whatif-cycle-2-1jwi0as.text: Over eons, the neighbours swallow that matter.

whatif-cycle-3-ggit27.text: One grows too big, destabilises… and bangs again.

whatif-cycle-4-w9si88.text: Our universe would be one breath in a great cosmic metabolism.

limits-0-251jgb.text: Let's be honest about what this is: a toy model.

limits-1-ij5atf.text: Newtonian gravity in flat space. No general relativity, no early universe, no microwave background spectrum, no baryon acoustic oscillations.

limits-2-yqc3p.text: It doesn't claim this is reality. It claims ordinary gravity can fake dark energy. And that's worth checking.

outro-0-8hlgj5.text: So. If the Hubble dipole, the Axis of Evil, and the dark flow all line up…

outro-1-129spza.text: …then dark energy might not be a property of space at all.

outro-2-p4tixh.text: It might just be the neighbours.
